setupGuides.title: Install Ubuntu using WSL
setupGuides.description: Run a Linux environment inside Windows without replacing Windows.

steps.heading: Check your Windows version
steps.instructions: Use a supported, updated Windows 10 or Windows 11 installation. Save your work before changing system settings.

steps.heading: Open PowerShell as Administrator
steps.instructions: Open the Start menu, search for PowerShell or Windows Terminal, right-click it and choose Run as administrator.
steps.warning: Only run installation commands from a trusted source.

steps.heading: Install WSL
steps.instructions: Run: wsl --install. Follow any prompts and restart Windows if asked.
steps.warning: The exact prompts can vary by Windows version and system configuration.

steps.heading: Open Ubuntu
steps.instructions: After installation, open Ubuntu from the Start menu. Allow the first-time setup to finish.

steps.heading: Create your Linux account
steps.instructions: Choose a Linux username and password. When typing the password, the terminal may not show characters; this is normal.

steps.heading: Update package information
steps.instructions: In Ubuntu, run: sudo apt update. Enter your Linux password if requested.

steps.heading: Verify your installation
steps.instructions: Try: whoami, pwd, uname -a and ls. If these commands return information, your Ubuntu terminal is ready.

setupGuides.title: Install Ubuntu using VirtualBox
setupGuides.description: Run Ubuntu in a virtual machine while keeping your existing operating system.

steps.heading: Prepare your computer
steps.instructions: Check available storage and memory. Back up important files before making system-level changes.

steps.heading: Get trusted installers
steps.instructions: Download VirtualBox from its official website and the Ubuntu Desktop ISO from Ubuntu's official website.

steps.heading: Create a virtual machine
steps.instructions: In VirtualBox, create a new Linux virtual machine and select the Ubuntu ISO as its installation image.

steps.heading: Allocate resources
steps.instructions: Choose memory, CPU and virtual disk settings that fit your computer. Avoid allocating all available resources.

steps.heading: Install Ubuntu
steps.instructions: Start the virtual machine and follow the Ubuntu installer. Review disk choices carefully; install inside the virtual disk, not your physical Windows drive.

steps.heading: Verify Ubuntu
steps.instructions: Open Terminal and run whoami, pwd and uname -a.

setupGuides.title: Install Linux using Dual Boot
setupGuides.description: Install Linux alongside an existing operating system and choose one when the computer starts.

steps.heading: Understand the risks
steps.instructions: Dual boot changes disk partitions and boot configuration. A mistake can cause data loss or make an operating system unbootable.
steps.warning: Back up important data first. This guide is educational, not a substitute for device-specific instructions.

steps.heading: Check compatibility
steps.instructions: Check your computer manufacturer's documentation, firmware mode, storage layout and Ubuntu's current installation guidance.

steps.heading: Prepare installation media
steps.instructions: Use the official Ubuntu ISO and a trusted tool to create a bootable USB drive.

steps.heading: Review disk layout
steps.instructions: Understand partitions and available unallocated space before proceeding. Do not delete or format a partition unless you know exactly what it contains.
steps.warning: Stop and seek expert help if you are unsure which partition is which.

steps.heading: Follow the official installer
steps.instructions: Use the current Ubuntu installation guide for your firmware and disk configuration. Review every disk and bootloader choice before confirming.

steps.heading: Test both operating systems
steps.instructions: Restart and verify that you can boot into both operating systems. Keep your recovery and backup options available.

lessons.title: What is Linux?
lessons.objective: Understand Linux, operating systems and Linux distributions.
lessons.mission: Understand Linux, operating systems and Linux distributions.

theory.heading: What is an operating system?
theory.content: An operating system (OS) is system software that manages computer hardware and provides services for applications. It helps programs use the CPU, memory, storage and input/output devices.
key_points: Applications run with the help of the OS.
Windows, macOS and Linux-based systems are examples.

theory.heading: What is Linux?
theory.content: Linux is technically an open-source operating system kernel. A complete Linux-based operating system combines the kernel with system tools, libraries and applications. These complete systems are commonly called Linux distributions.
key_points: The kernel manages communication between software and hardware.
Linux is used on desktops, servers, embedded devices and more.

theory.heading: What is a distribution?
theory.content: A Linux distribution packages the Linux kernel with software, tools and a package manager. Ubuntu, Fedora and Debian are examples. They share the Linux kernel but differ in defaults, release policies and tools.
key_points: Ubuntu is a distribution, not a separate kernel.

steps.title: Understand the environment
steps.text: A Linux system includes the kernel, system utilities, applications and a way for users to interact with it.
steps.hint: uname -s displays the operating-system kernel name.

steps.title: Identify the system
steps.text: Run uname -s in the practice terminal.
steps.hint: Use uname to display system information.

steps.title: Identify your user
steps.text: Find out which user is currently using the terminal.
steps.hint: The command name is a question: who am I?

challenge.title: Identify your Linux environment
challenge.instructions: Run whoami in the practice terminal.

lessons.title: Linux Distributions
lessons.objective: Compare distributions and understand why Ubuntu is used in this course.
lessons.mission: Compare distributions and understand why Ubuntu is used in this course.

theory.heading: Why are there different distributions?
theory.content: Different distributions select different software, desktop environments, package managers and update policies. This lets users choose a system that fits their needs.
key_points: Distributions share the Linux kernel family.
They may use different package managers.
Some prioritize stability while others prioritize newer software.

theory.heading: Ubuntu, Debian and Fedora
theory.content: Ubuntu is based on Debian and commonly uses APT for packages. Debian is known for its focus on stability. Fedora is associated with newer technologies and uses DNF.
key_points: Ubuntu and Debian use APT tools.

steps.title: Choose a distribution
steps.text: Ubuntu is a common beginner choice and has extensive documentation. The examples in this platform are Ubuntu-oriented.
steps.hint: This file contains operating-system identification information.

steps.title: Inspect system information
steps.text: Try the system identification command.
steps.hint: The -a option asks uname to show available system information.

steps.title: Check your current user
steps.text: Run whoami to identify the active account.

lessons.title: Terminal and Shell
lessons.objective: Understand the terminal, shell, command syntax and command options.
lessons.mission: Understand the terminal, shell, command syntax and command options.

theory.heading: Terminal vs shell
theory.content: A terminal is the interface where you type and view text. A shell is the program that reads commands and asks the operating system to carry them out. Bash is a commonly used shell on Ubuntu.
key_points: Bash is one example of a shell.

theory.heading: Command structure
theory.content: A command commonly has a command name followed by options and arguments. For example, ls -l /home asks ls to show a detailed listing of /home. Linux paths and command names are generally case-sensitive.
key_points: Argument: the item it acts on.
Uppercase and lowercase can mean different things.

steps.title: Read a command
steps.text: In ls -l /home, ls is the command, -l is an option and /home is an argument.
steps.hint: Options often begin with a hyphen.

steps.title: Run a command
steps.text: Use ls to list the current directory.

steps.title: Use a command option
steps.text: Display a detailed listing.

lessons.title: Essential Navigation Commands
lessons.objective: Identify the current location and move around the directory structure.
lessons.mission: Identify the current location and move around the directory structure.

theory.heading: Know where you are
theory.content: The shell keeps a current working directory. pwd prints its full path. This helps you understand where relative paths will be interpreted.
key_points: The home directory is commonly represented by ~.

theory.heading: List and move
theory.content: ls lists directory contents. cd changes the current directory. Use cd .. to move to the parent directory and cd ~ to return to your home directory.
key_points: clear clears the visible terminal screen.
history shows previously entered commands in many shells.

steps.title: Check your location
steps.text: Use pwd to display the current working directory.

steps.title: List the contents
steps.text: Use ls to see files and directories.

steps.title: Enter the docs folder
steps.text: Move into the docs directory.

lessons.title: Linux Directory Hierarchy
lessons.objective: Understand the root directory and common system directories.
lessons.mission: Understand the root directory and common system directories.

theory.heading: The root directory
theory.content: Linux organizes files in one tree that begins at /. This is the root directory. It is different from the root user's home directory, which is commonly /root.
key_points: / is the top of the filesystem tree.
/root is the root user's home directory.

theory.heading: Important directories
theory.content: /etc commonly stores system configuration, /var stores variable data such as logs, /tmp stores temporary files, and /bin contains essential command binaries on systems that use this layout.
key_points: /usr — many user-space programs and shared resources.

steps.title: Understand the tree
steps.text: Every absolute Linux path begins at /.

steps.title: Inspect your location
steps.text: Run pwd to see your current path.

steps.title: List your home directory
steps.text: Display the files and folders in your current home directory.

challenge.title: Explore the home directory
challenge.instructions: Run ls to inspect the current directory.

lessons.title: Paths and Hidden Files
lessons.objective: Distinguish absolute and relative paths and recognize hidden files.
lessons.mission: Distinguish absolute and relative paths and recognize hidden files.

theory.heading: Absolute and relative paths
theory.content: An absolute path starts from /. A relative path is interpreted from the current working directory. The special name . means the current directory and .. means its parent.

theory.heading: Hidden files
theory.content: On Linux, a filename beginning with a dot is treated as hidden by many directory-listing tools. Use ls -a to include hidden entries.
key_points: Hidden names begin with a dot.
A hidden file is not automatically secure.

steps.title: Compare paths
steps.text: If you are in /home/user, docs is a relative path and /home/user/docs is an absolute path.

steps.title: List hidden entries
steps.text: Use ls -a to include hidden entries.

steps.title: Move to the parent
steps.text: Move one directory up using ..

lessons.title: Creating and Managing Files
lessons.objective: Create directories and files, and understand copy, move and remove operations.
lessons.mission: Create directories and files, and understand copy, move and remove operations.

theory.heading: Directories and files
theory.content: mkdir creates directories and touch can create an empty file. cp copies files or directories, while mv moves or renames them. rm removes files; rmdir removes empty directories.
key_points: touch — create an empty file or update timestamps.

theory.heading: Be careful when deleting
theory.content: Removal commands can permanently delete data. In this learning platform, commands operate only on a simulated filesystem. On a real computer, check the path carefully before removing anything.
key_points: rm does not normally move files to a recycle bin.

steps.title: Create a directory
steps.text: mkdir creates a new directory in the current location.
steps.hint: mkdir is short for make directory.

steps.title: Create a directory
steps.text: Create a folder named practice.

steps.title: Create a file
steps.text: Create an empty file named hello.txt in your home directory.
steps.hint: Use touch followed by the filename.

lessons.title: Reading and Searching Files
lessons.objective: Read file contents, write simple text and search for files.
lessons.mission: Read file contents, write simple text and search for files.

theory.heading: Read file contents
theory.content: cat prints file contents. head displays the beginning of a file and tail displays the end. These are useful when a file is too long to inspect all at once.

theory.heading: Write and search
theory.content: echo prints text and can be combined with redirection to write output to a file. find searches for files and directories under a specified starting location.
key_points: > redirects output and overwrites a file.

steps.title: Read a file
steps.text: cat notes.txt displays the contents of notes.txt.

steps.title: Display file contents
steps.text: Read notes.txt.

steps.title: Write a message
steps.text: Write a short message into a file using echo and redirection.

lessons.title: Users and Groups
lessons.objective: Understand Linux accounts, groups and user identity.
lessons.mission: Understand Linux accounts, groups and user identity.

theory.heading: Users
theory.content: Linux is a multi-user operating system. Each user account has an identity and permissions. Processes generally run with the privileges of the user who started them.
key_points: A user account identifies a person or service.
id displays user and group identity information.

theory.heading: Groups
theory.content: Groups let administrators assign permissions to collections of users. A user can belong to one or more groups. The groups command displays the groups associated with the current user.
key_points: id shows user and group IDs.

steps.title: Identify the current user
steps.text: whoami displays the current effective username.

steps.title: Check your identity
steps.text: Run id to see user and group IDs.

steps.title: List your groups
steps.text: Display the groups associated with the current user.

lessons.title: Understanding File Permissions
lessons.objective: Read permission strings and understand owner, group and others.
lessons.mission: Read permission strings and understand owner, group and others.

theory.heading: Three permission categories
theory.content: Linux file permissions are commonly shown for three categories: owner, group and others. These categories determine which users can access a file or directory.
key_points: Group — users in the file's group.

theory.heading: Read, write and execute
theory.content: The letters r, w and x represent read, write and execute permissions. For a directory, execute permission is needed to access entries inside it. ls -l displays a long listing including permissions.

steps.title: Read a permission string
steps.text: In -rw-r--r--, the first character indicates file type, followed by permissions for owner, group and others.
steps.hint: Read the permission groups from left to right.

steps.title: Inspect permissions
steps.text: Run ls -l to view the simulated file permissions.

steps.title: Inspect the file
steps.text: Use ls -l to inspect the current directory in detail.

lessons.title: Changing Permissions with chmod
lessons.objective: Change permissions symbolically and understand numeric permission notation.
lessons.mission: Change permissions symbolically and understand numeric permission notation.

theory.heading: The chmod command
theory.content: chmod changes file or directory permissions. Symbolic notation uses categories such as u (owner), g (group), o (others) and operations such as + (add), - (remove) and = (set).
key_points: u = owner, g = group, o = others.
Example: chmod +x script.sh adds execute permission.

theory.heading: Numeric permissions
theory.content: Numeric permissions use 4 for read, 2 for write and 1 for execute. Add the values for each category. For example, 755 means owner has 7 (4+2+1), group has 5 (4+1), and others have 5 (4+1).
key_points: 755 = rwx for owner, r-x for group and others.
644 = rw- for owner, r-- for group and others.

steps.title: Add execute permission
steps.text: chmod +x notes.txt adds execute permission in the simulator.

steps.title: Change permissions
steps.text: Make notes.txt executable.

steps.title: Verify the permission
steps.text: Run ls -l after changing the permission.
steps.hint: Use ls -l to inspect the result.

lessons.title: Ownership, Root and sudo
lessons.objective: Understand file ownership and why administrative commands require care.
lessons.mission: Understand file ownership and why administrative commands require care.

theory.heading: Ownership
theory.content: Files and directories have an owning user and group. Ownership helps determine which permission set applies. chown is used to change ownership and normally requires administrative privileges.
key_points: Every file has an owner and group.

theory.heading: Root and sudo
theory.content: The root account has extensive administrative privileges. sudo allows an authorized user to run a command with elevated privileges. Use it carefully because administrative commands can change important system files.
key_points: sudo runs an authorized command with elevated privileges.
Do not copy privileged commands without understanding them.

steps.title: Understand administrative access
steps.text: sudo is used before a command when elevated privileges are required. The simulator explains this concept but does not grant real system access.

steps.title: Identify your user
steps.text: Run whoami to identify the active user.

steps.title: Inspect identity information
steps.text: Run id to inspect your user and group identity.

101.question: What is the main role of an operating system?
options: Manage hardware and provide services to applications
101.explanation: An operating system manages hardware resources and provides services to applications.

101.question: What is Linux technically?
101.explanation: Linux is technically an open-source operating system kernel.

101.question: Which component manages communication between software and hardware?
101.explanation: The kernel manages system resources and hardware interactions.

101.question: Which statement about Linux is correct?
options: It is only used on laptops
It is used in many kinds of devices and systems
101.explanation: Linux-based systems are used on servers, desktops, embedded devices and more.

102.question: What is a Linux distribution?
102.explanation: A distribution combines the Linux kernel with tools, software and defaults.

102.question: Which distribution is used for examples in this course?
Which package tool is commonly used by Ubuntu?
102.explanation: Ubuntu commonly uses APT for package management.

102.question: Which distribution commonly uses DNF?
102.explanation: Fedora uses DNF as its package manager.

102.question: Why do different distributions exist?
options: They have different software choices and goals
Linux requires a different CPU for each
102.explanation: Distributions make different choices about software, updates and defaults.

103.question: What is a terminal?
103.explanation: A terminal provides an interface for entering and viewing text commands.

103.question: What is a shell?
103.explanation: A shell reads commands and requests that the operating system carry them out.

103.question: Which is a commonly used shell?
103.explanation: Bash is a commonly used shell on Ubuntu.

103.question: In ls -l /home, what is -l?
103.explanation: -l is an option that changes the listing format.

103.question: Are Linux command names generally case-sensitive?
103.explanation: Linux command names and paths are generally case-sensitive.

104.question: Which command prints the current working directory?
104.explanation: pwd prints the current working directory.

104.question: Which command changes the current directory?
What does cd .. usually do?
104.explanation: The .. path component refers to the parent directory.

104.question: Which command clears the visible terminal screen?
104.explanation: clear clears the visible terminal screen.

201.question: Which symbol represents the root directory?
201.explanation: The root directory is represented by /.

201.question: Which directory commonly contains users' home directories?
Where are many system configuration files commonly stored?
Which directory commonly stores variable data and logs?
201.explanation: /var stores variable data, including many logs.

201.question: Is /root the same as /?
201.explanation: / is the filesystem root; /root is commonly the root user's home directory.

202.question: What does an absolute path begin with?
202.explanation: An absolute path starts from the root directory /.

202.question: A relative path is interpreted from where?
202.explanation: A relative path is interpreted from the current working directory.

202.question: What does .. represent in a path?
Which command includes hidden entries in a listing?
How do many Linux tools identify hidden filenames?
202.explanation: A filename beginning with a dot is treated as hidden by many tools.

203.question: Which command can create an empty file?
203.explanation: touch can create an empty file.

203.question: Which command copies files?
203.explanation: cp copies files and, with appropriate options, directories.

203.question: Which command moves or renames a file?
203.explanation: mv moves or renames files and directories.

204.question: Which command displays the beginning of a file?
204.explanation: head displays the beginning of a file.

204.question: Which command displays the end of a file?
204.explanation: tail displays the end of a file.

204.question: Which command searches for files and directories?
What does > do in shell redirection?
options: Redirects output and typically overwrites the target
204.explanation: The > operator redirects output and typically overwrites the target file.

301.question: Which command prints the effective username?
Which command displays user and group IDs?
301.explanation: id displays user and group identity information.

301.question: Which command lists groups for the current user?
Why are groups useful?
301.explanation: Groups let administrators assign access to multiple users together.

301.question: Is Linux designed to support multiple user accounts?
301.explanation: Linux is a multi-user operating system.

302.question: What does r represent in permissions?
Which groups are represented in a standard permission string?
302.explanation: The permission bits are shown for owner, group and others.

302.question: Which command shows a long listing with permissions?
302.explanation: ls -l displays a detailed listing including permissions.

303.question: What is the numeric value for read permission?
303.explanation: Read is represented by 4 in numeric permission notation.

303.question: What is the numeric value for write permission?
What is the numeric value for execute permission?

304.question: What is the root account?
options: An account with extensive administrative privileges
304.explanation: The root account has extensive administrative privileges.

304.question: What does sudo do?
options: Runs an authorized command with elevated privileges
304.explanation: sudo runs a command with elevated privileges when authorized.

304.question: Why should sudo be used carefully?
options: Privileged commands can change important system files
304.explanation: Administrative commands can affect important parts of the system.

304.question: Are ownership and permissions the same thing?
304.explanation: Ownership identifies the user and group; permissions define allowed access.
